Full Length Article
Hydrolysis and methane yield enhancement of anaerobic co-digestion of 
kitchen waste and sewage sludge by air/carbon dioxide nanobubble water
Qingfang Zhang a, Jiazi Niu a, Peilin Guo a, Jie Wang a, Cheng Peng a, Yifan Zhang a, Zhe Liu a,  
Yabian Wang b, Liyang Xue b, Tianfeng Wang a,*
a College of Petrochemical Engineering, Lanzhou University of Technology, Lanzhou 730050, China
b Gansu Provincial Ecological Environment Emergency and Accident Investigation Center, Lanzhou 730000, China
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Hybrid nanobubble water
System stability
Bacteria
Archaea
A B S T R A C T
Anaerobic co-digestion of kitchen waste and sewage sludge has attracted considerable attention, but the accu­
mulation of volatile fatty acid can affect biogas yield and hinder its application. In this study, the effects of air/ 
carbon dioxide nanobubble water (NBW) on hydrolysis and methane yield were investigated. Under mesophilic 
conditions, the addition of different NBW (Air, CO2, and Air + CO2) increased the total ammonia nitrogen in the 
hydrolysis stage by 6.6 %, 11.5 %, and 7.0 %, respectively. Meanwhile, the volatile fatty acid ratio total alkalinity 
of NBWAir+CO₂ was lower than that of the other NBW digesters, improving system stability. In addition, NBW 
increased ultimate methane yield by 4.7 %, 25.3 %, and 21.0 %, respectively. The addition of NBW also affected 
the microbial diversity and relative abundance of microorganisms in the digesters. The alpha diversity index of 
NBWAir+CO₂ is superior to other NBW digesters. Bacteria enriched with Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes, Proteobacteria, 
and Chloroflexi improved the hydrolysis, and methanogens were dominated by hydrotrophic types. In summary, 
the introduction of NBWAir+CO₂ provides new insights to improve hydrolysis, system stability, and methane yield 
efficiency.
1. Introduction
Kitchen waste (KW) in China is expected to exceed 103.0 million tons 
by 2025 [1]. The large amount of KW has caused a series of environ­
mental problems such as water pollution, garbage accumulation, odor 
pollution, etc., which need to be properly treated [2]. Anaerobic 
digestion (AD) is a cost-effective strategy to convert organic wastes such 
as KW into biogas for energy recovery [3]. However, when KW is the 
only substrate, the long-running AD process is susceptible to volatile 
fatty acid (VFA) inhibition, leading to poor performance or even failure 
of the AD [4]. This is mainly caused by the high carbon ratio nitrogen 
(C/N) of KW, and in this regard, anaerobic co-digestion has been pro­
posed to increase methane yield by adjusting C/N to an optimal level 
and supplementing deficient nutrients or trace elements [3].
Sewage sludge (SS) is a possible co-digestion substrate with KW since 
it has a lower C/N and slower hydrolysis rate. The efficiency of anaer­
obic co-digestion was higher than that of pure SS or pure KW at 
appropriate mixing ratios. At a 1:4 volatile solid (VS) ratio of KW and SS, 
methane yield was increased by 85.3 % compared with the digestion of 
KW alone [5]. In addition, higher methane recovery was observed at SS 
to KW mixing ratio of 1:1 (based on the dry VS), which resulted in a 4.6 
times higher methane yield, and a 3.9 times higher hydrolysis rate 
compared with SS mono-digestion [6]. Overall, the successful co- 
digestion of KW and SS confirms the superiority and the existence of 
synergistic effects that can accelerate the biodegradation process and 
recover methane more efficiently. Although co-digestion of KW and SS 
has attracted widespread focus, its further application still faces various 
unavoidable challenges, with a long lag phase, unstable performance, 
accumulation of VFA, and poor methane yield, which still need to be 
further optimized [1].
To address the above mentioned issues, many methods are available 
to increase methane yield and improve AD performance, such as pre­
treatment [7], biofortification [8], or digester optimization [9], which 
can be effective in mitigating inhibition. Even though the performance 
of AD is somewhat improved by these methods, the significant amount 
of chemicals added to AD increases the burden of ultimate waste treat­
ment, which may be too expensive on an industrial scale when combined 
with the development of secondary pollutants [10]. Consequently, it is

worthwhile to investigate an efficient and cost-effective solution strat­
egy to improve the stability and performance of co-digestion of these 
two substrates. Water is crucial in the AD process, not only as a major 
component of the digestive fluid but also to facilitate the transfer of 
hydrolysis products to sites where they can be utilized by bacteria [11]. 
However, relatively few studies have been conducted on the effects of 
different types and characteristics of water on AD performance.
Nanobubble water (NBW), as a green and pollution-free additive, has 
been used to enhance the AD performance of organic waste [12]. NBW 
has a large number of nano-sized bubbles [13]. Due to its large size of 
specific surface area, and small density, NBW has a superior sorption 
capacity and prolonged storage time that ordinary water does not have, 
which is enough to improve the reaction speed between gas and liquid 
and increase the activity of the organisms in the water [14]. The addi­
tion of NBWCO₂ to the AD of corn stover resulted in the highest cumu­
lative methane yield of 132.2 mL g−1 VSadded, which was 17.0 % higher 
than that of deionized water (DW) [15]. Meanwhile, the addition of 
NBWCO₂ accelerated the production and consumption of VFA. The 
addition of NBWAir increased H2 and methane yield by 38.0 % and 24.0 
% in the two-phase AD of KW [16]. These results demonstrate that 
different NBW gas species were utilized to promote the degradation of 
various substrates to enhance biogas yield.
Each NBW gas has unique properties that can produce different ef­
fects in the AD process. NBWAir addition may not only increase hydro­
lase activity at the end of the hydrolysis/acidification phase by inducing 
a microaerobic environment but also coenzyme activity at the end of the 
methanogenesis phase of the two-phase AD [17]. The addition of 
NBWCO₂ to the digesters increased the production of hydrogenotrophic 
methanogens, which in turn increased biogas yield [12]. In addition, 
CO2 can increase microbial diversity by generating bicarbonate, altering 
the community structure of methanogens [18]. NBWAir hybrid NBWCO₂ 
may provide both O2 and CO2, which promotes microbial metabolic 
activities and accelerates the degradation of organic matter. However, 
there are few studies on the effects of the hybrid application of NBW 
with these two gases on the AD process, and further research on this 
issue is needed to fully realize the potential for enhanced substrate 
degradation and overall biogas yield.
Therefore, this study investigated the effect of NBWAir, NBWCO₂, and 
their hybrid (NBWAir+CO₂) on the co-digestion of KW and SS; the per­
formance with or without NBW addition was evaluated by measuring 
the general parameters and observed the differences in methane yield 
and microbial community.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Substrate and inoculum
KW was collected from a university canteen in Lanzhou City, China. 
The collected KW was pretreated by sorting out plastic, bones, tissues, 
chopsticks, etc. The KW was then crushed and mixed, and the resulting 
paste was passed through a 0.25 mm sieve for spare use. SS was taken 
from a wastewater treatment plant in Lanzhou City, China, and the 
collection object was originally dewatered sludge, using the “oxidation 
ditch + aerated biofilter process”, with a scale of 5000.0 m3 d-1. The SS 
was recovered and domesticated in mesophilic (37 ± 2 ◦C) conditions 
and then used as inoculum. The characteristics of KW, SS, and inoculum 
are shown in Table 1.
2.2. Preparation of nanobubble water
The NBW in this study was prepared using a nanobubble generator 
(JXWNP-AL01, Jinxiang, China). Air and CO2 were introduced into DW 
via the generator, kept at 20 ± 2 ◦C for 20 min, and then left to stand for 
10 min to obtain NBW for use throughout the AD process. The pressure 
of the generator was controlled between 0.4–0.5 MPa during NBW 
preparation. Once prepared, the NBW is used in the ensuing AD process.
2.3. Anaerobic digestion experimental setup and Operation
The experimental setup consisted of a plexiglass digestion flask, a gas 
collection bag, a gas tube, a sampling tube, a filter head, and a water 
bath. The volume of the digester was 1 L. The digester setup used is the 
same as Liu et al [19]. To ensure smooth sampling, a filter head was 
connected to the inner part of the sampling metal tube to prevent 
sampling clogging, and the outer part of the tube was used for sampling 
and testing various parameters.
Based on the preliminary experiment, the optimum substrate mixing 
ratio was selected by mixing KW and SS in a 1:2 (VS) ratio, and 406 g 
was taken as substrate. Add inoculum to each digester with a ratio of 
inoculum to working volume of 1:5. With 261.0 g of DW as control, 
while 261.0 g of different types of NBW were added to a 1L digester as 
experimental groups with a total volume of 800 mL. The digesters were 
placed in a constant water bath at a temperature of 37 ± 2 ◦C for batch 
AD experiments. The four groups in this study were: the addition of DW, 
the addition of NBWAir, the addition of NBWCO₂, and the addition of 
NBWAir+CO₂. All experimental groups had four parallels. The bottles 
were gently shaken manually every day to ensure that the reaction was 
complete. On days 0, 3, 7, 14, 21, 29, and 40, a peristaltic pump was 
used to extract about 30.0 g of digestate for analysis.
2.4. Methods of analysis
The digestate is centrifuged at 2000 g for 10 min and the liquid su­
pernatant is strained through a 0.45 μm polyethersulfone ultrafine fiber 
filter. The parameters are determined using the strained liquid. Total 
solid (TS), VS, soluble chemical oxygen demand (SCOD), total ammonia 
nitrogen (TAN), and total alkalinity (TA) were determined using stan­
dard methods [20]. The pH was determined using a handheld high 
precision pH meter. The meter was calibrated with a standard solution 
before use and readings were recorded after stabilization. Free ammonia 
nitrogen (FAN) in liquid samples is measured by a standard formula 
[21]. Concentrations of VFA (acetic, propionic, isobutyric, n-butyric, 
isovaleric, and n-valeric acids) were determined by using a gas chro­
matograph (SP-7890 Plus, Rui Hong, China) equipped with an organic 
acid analytical column (30.0 m long, 320.0 µm internal diameter, 0.5 µm 
film) and a hydrogen flame ionization detector. The amount of biogas 
was determined by a gas flow meter (LML-2, Alpha, China). Methane 
concentration in the biogas was assessed using a biogas analyzer 
(GA5000, Geotach, UK).
Deoxyribonucleic acid was extracted from digestate, and the mi­
croorganisms contained therein were tested for abundance and type 
using high-throughput sequencing to determine differences in the mi­
crobial community in the digesters after the addition of different NBW. 
Primers 341F (5′-CCTACGGGAGGCAGCAG-3′) and 806R (5′-GGAC­
TACHVGGGGTWTCTAAT-3′) were utilized to amplify the bacterial 16S 
rRNA gene in the V3-V4 portion of the bacterial 16S rRNA gene; using 
primers Arch519F (5′-CAGCCGCCGCGGTAA-3′) and Arch915R (5′-

2.5. Statistical analysis
Data were analyzed using SPSS for Windows system version 27.0. 
Data between different experimental groups were analyzed using 
ANOVA (analysis of variance) and differences between two experi­
mental groups were considered to exist when p < 0.05. In addition, 
principal component analysis (PCA) and Duncan’s test were performed. 
Methane yield is fitted using a modification of the Gompertz model. 
Spearman correlation analysis was performed between microbial rela­
tive abundance (RA) and environmental factors in the experiment.
3. Results and Discussion
3.1. Digestion performance
The pH is a key factor in the AD process and directly affects the 
stability of the AD system [15]. During the start of the AD process, a 
rapid decrease in pH occurs in all digesters owing to the amount of acid 
during the acid production phase. This second decrease can be attrib­
uted to the organic matter released by the microbial cells in an alkaline 
environment [22]. Throughout the reaction phase, the pH is maintained 
between 6.5–7.8, within the normal range of the AD process (6.5–8.2) 
[23].
Typically, SCOD increases with hydrolysis and acidification and is 
partially removed as methanogens consume organic acids, converting 
them into methane and carbon dioxide, therefore the difference in SCOD 
is closely related to biogas yield [14]. The SCOD in different experi­
mental groups showed a similar trend of increasing first and then 
decreasing (Fig. 1b). On day 3, the SCOD reached the maximum, which 
may have been caused by the release of a large amount of VFA during the 
hydrolysis stage. At this time, the SCOD in the NBW groups was higher 
than that in the DW group, indicating that the addition of NBW could 
promote the hydrolysis of co-digestion of KW and SS, and the highest 
SCOD increased by 5.7 %, 10.4 % (p < 0.05) and 8.5 % in the digesters of 
NBWAir, NBWAir, and NBWAir+CO₂. After day 3, the SCOD began to 
decrease. It is noteworthy that the NBWAir+CO₂ groups had the highest 
rate of decrease in SCOD during this period, 79.9 %, which was superior 
to DW (78.7 %), NBWAir (78.1 %), and NBWCO₂ (78.8 %), and this 
phenomenon suggests that the hybrid NBW facilitates the decomposition 
of organic matter. After day 29, the second increase in SCOD implies that 
the microorganisms ruptured in the highly alkaline environment, 
releasing organic matter [22].
TAN is a result of the hydrolysis of proteins and is used to reaction

the hydrolysis performance of AD [19]. Low levels of TAN can provide 
cushioning and nutrition for microbial, however high levels can inhibit 
the growth of methanogens [24]. In the early stage of the AD process, the 
TAN in each digester gradually increased and then stabilized (Fig. 1c). 
This may be due to the decomposition of proteins in the early stage of 
AD, which increases the amount of inorganic nitrogen such as ammonia 
nitrogen. TAN in all digesters reached 1918.0–2005.8 mg L-1 at the end 
of AD, suggesting that ammonia inhibition may be occurring in DW and 
NBW when the rate of methane yield slows [25]. The TAN in the 
experimental groups was higher than those in previous studies, which 
may be caused by different substrates and NBW addition to promote 
hydrolase activity [26]. On day 3, NBWAir, NBWCO₂, and NBWAir+CO₂ 
significantly increased TAN by 6.6 % (p < 0.01), 11.5 % (p < 0.001), and 
7.0 % (p < 0.001), respectively, as compared with the DW, with sig­
nificant differences between groups. This result suggests that TAN is 
more affected by different NBW during the hydrolysis stage. In addition, 
NBWAir and NBWAir+CO₂ showed an increase of 4.6 % (p < 0.05) and 4.5 
% (p < 0.05) on day 40, whereas NBWCO₂ (3.1 %) showed no significant 
difference. This suggests that NBWAir and NBWAir+CO₂ played an equal 
role in the methanogenic stage, while NBWCO₂ did not play a significant 
role. This may be due to the fact that NBWAir generates a large amount of 
reactive oxygen species, which improves the digestibility of the sub­
strate and thus promotes the oxidation of organic matter [12].
FAN can penetrate microbial cell membranes and cause proton im­
balances or toxic cytoplasmic enzymes [14]. Therefore, the toxicity of 
FAN is greater than that of ionic ammonia. As AD proceeded, FAN 
gradually increased (Fig. 1d). After day 29, the FAN in DW, NBWCO₂, and 
NBWAir+CO₂ decreased, which may be due to a decrease in pH. Since the 
pH of NBWAir+CO₂ is lower, although the TAN is higher than in other 
NBW digesters, the FAN is also lower. When FAN exceeds 250.0 mg L-1, 
methanogens are affected [22]. In this experiment, the FAN in all di­
gesters consistently remained below the threshold.
VFA are the products of acid generation and methanogenic substrates 
in the AD process. It is an essential index of the stability and function of 
the AD system [27]. The trend of VFA was similar to that of SCOD, both 
showing a trend of increasing and then decreasing (Fig. 2). The high 
concentration of VFA was almost completely consumed from day 7 to 
day 40 and the study showed a similar trend of VFA degradation [24]. 
Digesters VFA added with NBW accumulated more in the early stage, 
providing more feedstock for methanogens. On day 3, the VFA peaked 
and was mainly dominated by propionic acid, its higher concentrations 
(1000.0–2000.0 mg L-1) are susceptible to methanogens [28]. At this 
time, NBWAir had the highest concentration of VFA, which was incon­
sistent with the trend of SCOD, probably because some of the VFA in the 
NBWCO₂ and NBWAir+CO₂ digesters had already been utilized by metha­
nogens and converted to methane [15]. As fermentation progressed, 
NBWAir+CO₂ had lower levels of acid accumulation in the VFA. These 
results suggest that the addition of hybrid NBW facilitates the 
consumptive use of VFA for methane conversion, which restores the 
stabilization of the AD system.
TA is related to the buffering capacity of the digesters [29]. As 
fermentation proceeded, the TA in each digester gradually increased, 
indicating enhanced buffering capacity (Fig. 3a). After day 3, the TA in 
all the digesters with NBW addition was higher than in DW, suggesting 
that the addition of NBW promotes the production of TAN and thus 
increases the TA, which may play an important role in restoring the 
stabilization of the acidic AD system.
The VFA ratio TA (VFA/TA) is already used in the AD system as a key 
indicator for evaluating the stabilization of the AD process, with ratios 
greater than 0.4 indicating an unstable AD process [14]. In the early 
stage, the VFA/TA of all digesters ranged from 1.9 to 2.0, which was 
higher than the threshold value, and DW was the lowest (Fig. 3b). This 
indicates that at the beginning of the AD process, the digesters were in 
an unstable state. As AD proceeded to day 7, the VFA/TA of all digesters 
decreased, with the NBWAir and NBWCO₂ groups higher than the DW by 
13.3 % and 9.3 %, while the NBWAir+CO₂ groups which were significantly 
lower than that of DW by 24.3 % (p < 0.001), and this change suggests 
that NBWAir+CO₂ can effectively promote the early recovery of digesters 
stability, which is important for alleviating the acid inhibition phe­
nomenon during the AD process [26].

3.2. Methane yield
The Gompertz model is suitable for co-digestion systems [30]. The 
model was used to fit the cumulative methane yield (CMY) and the re­
sults are shown for the lag phase (λ), maximum methane production rate 
(Rm), and ultimate methane yield (UMY) (Table 2). λ determines bac­
terial adaptation to the digester and biogas yield [31]. The NBWAir λ was 
the shortest, however, only 246.78 ± 1.96 mL g−1 VSadded methane was 
recovered at the end. For NBWCO₂, λ was about 3.8 d, which may be due 
to the adaptation of microorganisms to the supplement. NBWAir+CO₂ was 
adversely affected by 4.6 d, which was not different from the DW. A 
longer λ is acceptable if high biogas and methane yield is achieved [31].
Three peaks of Rm occurred in all groups (Fig. 4a). The first peak 
appeared on day 1–2 of co-digestion, and may be caused by the degra­
dation of biodegradable organic matter [1]. The second peak occurred 
on day 4–7 and may be caused by the large amounts of acetic and butyric 
acids during methanogenesis. The last peak occurred on day 13–17 and 
may be caused by the transformation of propionic acid to acetic acid for 
use by methanogens [27]. During the early stage (day 0–2), the Rm 
increased from 0.0 to 7.5–9.3 mL g−1 VSadded d-1. However, Rm was 
unstable from day 2 to day 8 due to the accumulation of VFA. After 
adapting to the environment, Rm increased steadily. It was also found 
that the digesters with DW and NBWAir reached the highest Rm on day 
16, whereas NBWCO₂ and NBWAir+CO₂ on day 14, suggesting that NBWCO₂ 
and NBWAir+CO₂ have a certain shortening effect on the startup of the 
digesters to speed up the adaptation of anaerobic microorganisms to the 
environment. NBWAir is inconsistent with previous studies, which may 
be due to differences in substrates [16]. During AD, NBWAir+CO₂ had the 
largest Rm, which was significantly different from the DW, with an 
improvement of 39.1 % (p < 0.01).
The trend in CMY for digesters with NBW or DW added increased 
steadily with digestion duration (Fig. 4b). Overall, UMY was higher in 
NBW digesters than DW, and according to Duncan’s analysis, the NBW 
groups were significantly different from DW. UMY increased by 4.7 % (p 
< 0.05), 25.3 % (p < 0.001), and 21.0 % (p < 0.001) in the digesters with 
the addition of NBWAir, NBWCO₂ and NBWAir+CO₂, respectively. NBWCO₂ 
and NBWAir+CO₂ were also significantly different from NBWAir, being 
19.7 % (p < 0.001) and 15.6 % (p < 0.001) higher than NBWAir in both 
groups, whereas NBWCO₂ did not show a statistically significant differ­
ence from NBWAir+CO₂. Where NBWAir is due to the presence of a 
microaerobic environment and increased activity of hydrolyzing and 
acid-producing microorganisms in the digesters, which promotes sub­
strate hydrolysis [17]. NBWCO₂ has the highest UMY probably since CO2 
is a readily soluble gas and more CO2 in biogas can dissolve in water by 
forming NH4HCO3 under high pH and TAN conditions, which increases 
the methane production in the NBWCO₂ digesters [15]. In addition, CO2 
can be used as a substrate to promote the production of hydro­
genotrophic methanogens using H2 molecules as electron donors [12]. If 
the influence of removing CO2 itself is to be considered, assuming 
complete conversion of CO2, it can be calculated by the mass balance 
that the CO2 added to the NBWCO₂ group theoretically converts 11.9 mL 
g−1 VSadded methane, yet NBWCO₂ was higher than DW 59.7 mL g−1 
VSadded in this study, which suggests that the introduction of NBWCO₂ 
generates bicarbonate to increase microbial diversity and change the 
community structure of methanogens [15].
In the present study, several parallel experiments showed that the 
addition of NBW promoted UMY (Fig. 4) and digestion stability (Fig. 3b) 
during AD. NBWAir+CO₂ combines the advantages of the above 
mentioned two gases, which not only improves UMY performance but 
also provides a more cost-effective option for methane yield by using 
only half the cost of NBWCO₂.
In the previous, methane yield increased by 20.8 % and 19.1 % for 
NBWAir and NBWCO₂, which was higher and lower than the present study 
[11]. This may be due to the different substrates. The addition of NBWAir 
acted as a buffer, enhancing the buffering and resilience of the AD sys­
tem and accelerating the production and consumption of reducing 
sugars and VFA [17]. Nanobubbles have high gas solubility, which fa­
cilitates the dissolution of more CO2 and thus improves the buffering 
performance of the NBWCO₂ [15]. NBW increases water mobility in the 
surrounding aquatic environment, thereby enhancing microorganism 
activity. By increasing water mobility, the mass transfer of nutrients to

3.3. Characteristics of the microbial community
3.3.1. Diversity of microbial community
The OTUs, Shannon and Chao1 indexes of bacterial sequences were 
larger and Simpson indexes were smaller in all the digesters of this 
study, indicating that bacterial diversity and RA were much higher than 
archaea (See supplementary material). According to Duncan’s test, 
the OTUs, Shannon, and Chao1 indexes of bacteria in digesters with 
NBW addition were significantly higher than DW during the methano­
genic stage (day 21), which may be attributed to the higher delivery 
efficiency of NBW gas and its potential to penetrate the inner regions of 
bioflocs and biofilms due to its small size and relative stability, allowing 
them to be transported in the cells [32]. Among the three NBW, the 
OTUs, Shannon, and Chao1 indexes of the bacterial sequences in the 
digesters with NBWAir+CO₂ added were higher than those of the other 
NBW, suggesting that the different gaseous NBW also affected the spe­
cies richness of bacteria.
3.3.2. The distributions of bacterial sequences
Bacteria were dominated at the phylum level by Firmicutes, Bacter­
oidetes, Proteobacteria, and Chloroflexi (Fig. 5a and Fig. 5b). During the 
methanogenic stage (day 21), the RA of Firmicutes increased and Bac­
teroidetes decreased in all digesters.
Firmicutes can decompose a wide range of complex organic matter, 
including proteins and carbohydrates, and are active in both mesophilic 
and thermophilic conditions [31]. The RA is the highest in the early and 
late stages of AD. It ranges from 36.6 %-43.0 % on day 3 and increases to 
39.2 %-52.3 % on day 21. Firmicutes can form endospores, allowing 
them to endure unfavorable external conditions and survive in 
extremely harsh environments [33]. On day 3, the accumulation of VFA 
is severe in all digesters, which is not conducive to the multiplication 
and metabolism of microorganisms. However, Firmicutes adapt and 
become the dominant microorganisms in the community. After corre­
lation analysis of bacteria with environmental factors, there is a negative 
correlation between Firmicutes and VFA (p < 0.001, R = -0.73), SCOD (p 
< 0.001, R = -0.76) (Fig. 5c). Compared with the DW, the RA of Fir­
micutes in the groups with added NBW is lower, indicating that the 
addition of NBW can alleviate the acidic inhibition in the digesters. The 
RA of Firmicutes grew faster in NBWCO₂ and NBWAir+CO₂ compared with 
NBWAir, a higher RA of Firmicutes can promote the hydrolysis and 
acidification of organic matter [28].
In comparison, another important member in the hydrolysis and 
acidification process is Bacteroidetes. Bacteroidetes are responsible for 
degrading cellulose and various proteins into fatty acids and ammonia 
[28]. On day 21, the RA of Bacteroidetes in the groups with added NBW is 
higher than DW, indicating that the addition of NBW promotes hydro­
lysis more effectively. The primary role of Bacteroidetes in AD is hy­
drolysis and acidification, so their RA is high in the early stage of AD and 
decreases with the end of hydrolysis [22]. Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes 
are closely associated with the hydrolysis and acidification of organic 
matter, with their RA showing a negative correlation [34]. During the 
AD process, the RA of Firmicutes increases, while the RA of Bacteroidetes 
decreases markedly.
Proteobacteria is a phylum often found in the AD process, and its main 
function is to decompose a large amount of organic matter and digest 
some VFA [35]. It plays a significant role in the late stage of digesting 
propionate in the digesters. As digestion progresses, the RA of Proteo­
bacteria in the DW group decreases. Adding NBWAir, NBWCO₂, and 
NBWAir+CO₂ to the digesters can effectively increase the RA of Proteo­
bacteria, enhance hydrolysis, and lead to an increase in methane yield. 
Chloroflexi is capable of degrading a wide range of complex 
macromolecules, including proteins and carbohydrates [36]. In the early 
stage of AD, the RA of Chloroflexi is between 2.5 %–5.4 %, and it rises to 
6.9 %–12.7 % on day 21. This indicates that as AD progresses, the 
structure of the microbial community becomes more conducive to the 
enrichment of functional microorganisms, thereby accelerating the hy­
drolysis and acidification process of co-digestion with KW and SS. The 
dominant phylum of sludge in AD includes Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes, 
Actinobacteria, Proteobacteria, Chloroflexi, and Spirochaetes, with Firmi­
cutes being the most prevalent in digesters such as restaurants and feces, 
which is consistent with the present study [37].
Bacteria were further analyzed at the genus level (See supplemen­
tary material). On day 3, the dominant genus in AD were Streptococcus, 
Bacteroides, and Macellibacteroides. On day 21, Syntrophomonas, and 
Macellibacteroides dominated. Streptococcus is primarily responsible for 
converting sugar to lactic acid [38]. The enrichment of Streptococcus in 
all digesters promoted the accumulation of acid. Streptococcus had a 
significantly negative correlation with methane yield (p < 0.001, R =
-0.83), and the RA of Streptococcus in the digesters with NBW added was 
lower than that of DW on day 3, suggesting that NBW could enhance the 
metabolic activity of methanogens and thus increase methane yield. 
Streptococcus was less susceptible to the effects of AD, and the lower RA 
of Streptococcus in NBW digesters indicated that the addition of NBW 
was effective in mitigating the damage to the digesters by Streptococcus 
[39]. The decrease in the RA of Streptococcus on day 21 was probably 
due to the degradation of VFA in the digesters.
Syntrophomonas can be enriched upon contact with VFA and can 
establish a syntonic metabolism with methanogens [4]. Thus, Syntro­
phomonas was enriched during AD, with RA increasing to 20.2 %-27.2 
%. There was a significantly positive correlation with CMY (p < 0.001, R 
= 0.75). Bacteroides perform an influential role in the hydrolysis of 
several polysaccharides and the production of VFA by AD [40]. It had a 
significantly positive correlation with VFA (p < 0.001, R = 0.78). On day 
3, the RA of Bacteroides in NBWAir+CO₂ was 15.1 %, which was lower than 
the DW, which may explain the lesser VFA in the added NBWAir+CO₂ 
digesters. As digestion proceeded, the RA of Bacteroides gradually 
decreased and VFA was gradually consumed. Macellibacteroides can 
utilize monosaccharides to produce VFA, promote the conversion of 
proteins and carbohydrates to soluble sugars and VFA, and accelerate 
hydrolysis and acid production [41]. Its RA decreased from 9.2 %-11.9 
% to 3.8 %-4.9 % during the AD process, when VFA was rapidly 
consumed.
PCA plot revealed differences between bacterial communities 
(Fig. 5d). At the hydrolysis stage, the addition of NBW differed from the 
DW, indicating that the addition of different NBW affected the activity of 
microorganisms. However, the difference was not significant in the 
methanogenic stage, which may be due to the slower change of the 
bacterial community in the late stage of AD [42].
3.3.3. The distributions of archaea sequences
Methanogens are archaea that perform an influential role in the 
carbon cycle in nature [43]. During the AD process, methanogens are 
more susceptible to external elements than bacteria, which may lead to 
changes in the function of archaea in response to changing environ­
mental conditions [44]. The archaeal community at the phylum level 
consisted mainly of Euryarchaeota and Nanoarchaeaota (See supple­
mentary material).
The RA of Euryarchaeota in the digesters (67.6 %-74.8 %) tended to 
increase with AD time in the same reactor (98.6 %-99.4 %). Eur­
yarchaeota is a fastidious and strict anaerobe that utilizes CO2 for energy 
production and carbon fixation via the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway (WLP) 
[45]. In this pathway, most bacteria (acetate-producing bacteria) pro­
duce acetate as an end product, while most archaea (CO2-reducing 
methanogens) produce methane [46]. WLP application studies include 
(1) promotion of acetic acid production or chain elongation by injection 
of exogenous H2 and CO2, biogas recirculation, or addition of zero- 
valent iron to convert VFA to medium-chain fatty acids, and (2)

stimulation of CO2 utilization by CO2-reducing methanogens to drive 
methanogenic [47]. The presence of Firmicutes, Proteobacteria with 
Euryarchaeota in the digesters is justified by the fact that the product 
“hydrogen” released by them is used by the hydrogenotrophic metha­
nogens in Euryarchaeota for methane yield. Therefore, Firmicutes, Pro­
teobacteria, and Euryarchaeota should co-exist in the methane production 
process. Nanoarchaeaota is highly adaptable to harsh environments [2].
Further analyses were carried out at the genus level to gain insight 
into the structure of the archaeal community. In the early stage of AD, 
the digesters are dominated by three types of archaeal genus, Meth­
anobacterium, Methanocorpusculum, and Methanobrevibacter. As AD pro­
ceeded, Methanobacterium became the only dominant genus (Fig. 6a and 
Fig. 6b).
Methanobacterium is a strict hydrogenotrophic methanogen, utilizing 
H2 and CO2 to produce methane [31]. Among all the digesters, Meth­
anobacterium was enriched (53.5 %-56.6 %), and its RA increased to 
92.1 %-96.1 % as digestion proceeded. The addition of NBW promoted 
the enrichment of Methanobacterium in the late stage of digestion, which 
was a significantly positive correlation with CMY (p < 0.001, R = 0.76) 
(Fig. 6c), suggesting that the addition of NBW could enhance the sym­
biosis between other bacteria and hydrogenotrophic methanogens, 
which in turn increased the methane yield. The RA of Methanobacterium 
was higher under microaerobic conditions, which was consistent with 
the present study [48].
Methanocorpusculum is commonly used in methanogenic bioreactor 
assays and is found in high RA in many leachates, where it can utilize 
H2/CO2 or formate as a substrate for methanogenesis [44]. In addition, 
Methanocorpusculum had a negative correlation with CMY (p < 0.01, R =
-0.59), and its RA gradually decreased in the late stage of AD. Meth­
anobrevibacter is also a hydrogenotrophic methanogenic bacterium with 
high acid tolerance [4]. The RA of Methanobrevibacter in the NBW- 
added digesters was higher on day 3, and had a positive correlation 
with VFA (p < 0.001, R = -0.79), suggesting that the introduction of 
NBW improved the hydrolysis of AD. As the VFA was consumed, the RA 
of Methanobrevibacter decreased to 0.3 %-0.5 %.
Methanomassiliiccoccus is a hydrogenotrophic and methylotrophic 
methanogen [2]. In the methanogenic stage, the RA of NBWAir+CO₂ was 
1.0 %, and the other groups were less than 1.0 %, indicating that the 
enrichment of methanogens by hybrid NBW was more significant. In 
summary, a lower diversity of methanogenic flora was observed when 
the digesters treated KW and SS. This low diversity usually indicates a 
more sensitive and unstable ecosystem [49].
There are some differences in the PCA plot of the hydrolysis and 
methanogenic phases of the archaeal community (Fig. 6d), but the dis­
tances between the groups are similar, which is mainly due to the low 
diversity of the archaea.
4. Conclusion
The addition of NBW promoted hydrolysis and increased methane 
yield. The methane yield of NBWAir, NBWCO₂, and NBWAir+CO₂ increased 
by 4.7 %, 25.3 %, and 21.0 %. The addition of NBWAir+CO₂ improved the 
stability of digestion, decomposed organic matter most thoroughly, 
alleviated the inhibition caused by the accumulation of VFA, and facil­
itated the subsequent methanation process. The addition of NBW 
increased the RA of methanogens, which, together with hydro­
genotrophic methanogens, improved the utilization of hydrogen, 
thereby increasing methane yield. In addition, NBWAir+CO₂ is inexpen­
sive and has the potential for large-scale diffusion in industry.
